title: Anatomy of a JWT
summary: Three base64url parts separated by dots. Implement base64url yourself and decode a real token.

steps.title: Three parts and two dots
body: A **JSON Web Token** (JWT, said "jot", RFC 7519) is a compact, signed bundle of claims. Here is a real one:
It is three parts joined by `.`:
- **Header**: JSON saying how the token is signed: `{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}`
- **Signature**: bytes computed over `header.payload` with a key. Change one character of the first two parts and it no longer matches.

The header and payload are **encoded, not encrypted**. Anyone holding the token can read every claim. The signature makes the token *tamper-evident*, not secret. Never put a password, a card number or anything private in a JWT payload.

Why use them? A server that receives a JWT can check it **without a database lookup**: verify the signature, read the claims, done. That makes them popular between services and for APIs, and it is also the root of their main weakness (they are hard to revoke), which you will meet at the end of this module.

steps.prompt: Ada copies her JWT from the browser's dev tools. What can she do with it?
options: Read every claim in the payload, but not change one without breaking the signature
Change her role to admin, as long as she re-encodes the payload correctly
Read the claims only if she knows the signing key
steps.explain: Base64url is just an encoding. Reading is free; forging needs the key. (Encrypted JWTs exist, called JWE, but the everyday JWT is a signed JWS.)

steps.title: base64url
body: Tokens travel in URLs, headers and cookies, so they use **base64url** (RFC 4648 §5), a URL-safe variant of base64:
In C#, take the normal base64 and fix it up:
Step through it below with three bytes chosen to produce both awkward characters.

steps.explain: Two bytes need one `=` of padding in base64; base64url drops it. `251, 255, 191` encodes to `+/+/`, which becomes `-_-_`.

steps.title: Decoding: put the padding back
body: `Convert.FromBase64String` insists on padding, so decoding reverses the steps and pads the length up to a multiple of 4:
case 1: throw new FormatException("Not valid base64url.");
A remainder of 1 can never happen in valid base64 (one leftover character holds only 6 bits, not a whole byte), so it means the input is broken.

steps.explain: Swap the URL-safe characters back, reject impossible lengths, pad to a multiple of 4, then decode. `(4 - len % 4) % 4` is 0, 2 or 1 extra characters.

steps.title: Implement base64url
prompt: - `byte[] FromB64Url(string text)`: throws `FormatException` when the length leaves a remainder of 1 after dividing by 4.
solution: case 1: throw new FormatException("Not valid base64url.");
hints: Decode: swap the characters back, add `==` for remainder 2 and `=` for remainder 3.
template: Dojo.Eq("round trip of 50 bytes", dojoRandom, FromB64Url(B64Url(dojoRandom)));

steps.prompt: The issuer built this token's middle part from the JSON `{"sub":"ada","exp":1700000900}`. The program below has no key. What does it print?
steps.explain: Decoding the middle part needs no key at all. That is why a payload must never hold secrets.

steps.title: Decode a token
prompt: Write `(string Header, string Payload) Decode(string jwt)` that returns the header and payload as JSON text.
- Throw `FormatException` if the token doesn't have exactly three parts.
Your `B64Url` and `FromB64Url` aren't provided: include a decoder in your code.
Note the empty third part: that is a valid *shape*, even though a token with `alg: none` must never be trusted.
solution: case 1: throw new FormatException("Not valid base64url.");
if (parts.Length != 3) throw new FormatException("A JWT has three parts.");
template: Dojo.Eq("the sample token's payload", "{\"sub\":\"ada\",\"name\":\"Ada Lovelace\",\"iat\":1700000000}", dojoD.Payload);
Dojo.Eq("non-ASCII text survives", "{\"name\":\"Zoë\"}", Decode(DojoJwt.Hs("{\"name\":\"Zoë\"}", new byte[32])).Payload);
